title: How to Spot and Block Fake Bank Text Message Alerts
bigPicture: Real banks will never ask for your password or PIN through a text message — if a text feels wrong, it probably is.
whatYouNeedToKnow: Fake texts often say your account is locked or there is suspicious activity to scare you into clicking fast.
Real bank texts usually just tell you to call the number on the back of your card or log in through the official app.
A fake link may look almost real but has small misspellings like 'b0famerica' instead of 'bankofamerica'.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Clicking the link inside the text message — even if it looks urgent.
Replying 'STOP' to a suspicious text — this just tells the scammer your number is active.
Calling a phone number provided in the text instead of using the one on your card or bank statement.
actionSteps: Pause and breathe — scammers rely on panic. Take 30 seconds before doing anything.
Call your bank directly using the number on your debit card or official website.
Forward the fake text to 7726 (SPAM) to help your carrier block it.
Block the sender in your phone's messaging app.
Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
